_schema: Gate 1 Tier A — national tests. Methodology §2.1. Tests A1, A2, A4 are binary gates; A3 is scored 0-1 (see §2.1 rationale). A4 is PRESENT TENSE as of the v1.1 amendment: it asks whether a gold-control regime is in operation, not whether one ever was. Dormant statutory powers and historical use are recorded per country and carried as disclosed residual risk (§11.1), not gated. A2 is measured on the CURRENCY ISSUER and carries a gross-debt limb as of the v1.2 amendment: see tests.A2_solvency and the Canada record for why, and note that the amendment CHANGED the rule rather than sourcing the old one.

tests.A1_monetary_sovereignty: Own currency; freely floating; not a global reserve currency; not in a currency union. BINARY.
tests.A2_solvency: Measured on the CURRENCY ISSUER — the national government — not on the consolidated general government. Three limbs, all binary, all on one named vintage: net debt/GDP <= 60% AND gross debt/GDP <= 85% AND interest/revenue <= 10%. A country fails A2 if it breaches any one. General-government figures are recorded alongside for context and are not the test. See §2.1 'Rationale for A2' for why the consolidation level and the gross limb are specified: A1 already scopes Gate 1 to the entity that issues the currency, and A2 asks whether that same entity has a fiscal motive to reach for the metal. A province cannot print, cannot impose exchange control and cannot requisition bullion, so its balance sheet does not answer the question. Netting is not permitted against social-security fund assets, assets of another level of government, or any earmarked or illiquid asset: a pension fund's equity portfolio does not service the sovereign's coupon. The gross limb exists because gross debt is what must be ROLLED, and rollover at rising rates is the transmission channel from solvent-on-paper to reaching-for-the-metal.
tests.A2_threshold_note: 85% gross is set where the recorded cross-section leaves a gap, and is disclosed as such rather than derived from theory — the same construction as constraints.single_asset_pp_share_threshold, which sits at 0.80 because nothing in that cross-section falls between 0.773 and 0.999. Here nothing recorded falls between Australia at ~61% general government (~36% Commonwealth) and Canada at ~105-110%. The Maastricht 60% gross reference value was considered first, as the externally-anchored choice that could not be accused of being tuned, and REJECTED on measurement: at the IMF's general-government basis Australia reads ~61% and would fail, which would leave the index with no eligible jurisdiction and reproduce the exact v1.0 A4 defect — a rule that vetoes the asset class is a decision not to run the product, disguised as a test (§2.1). The threshold applies prospectively and evenly. If Australian general government gross debt reaches 85%, Australia fails A2 and there is nothing left to hold.
tests.A3_gold_as_export: Gold's share of national goods exports. SCORED 0-1, not gated — failing means the state has no stake in defending you, not that it will expropriate.
tests.A4_gold_controls_in_operation: No confiscation, compulsory delivery, administered monopsony or gold-export prohibition IN FORCE at the review date, verified against primary law. BINARY. Dormant powers and historical use do NOT fail this test; they are recorded in `dormant_powers` / `history` and disclosed under §11.1. See §2.1 for why the v1.0 formulation — which gated on history and on suspended-not-repealed powers — was withdrawn: Australia failed it, and was recorded PASS anyway.

countries.name: Australia

A1.note: AUD freely floating, non-reserve, commodity-linked. A small open commodity currency devalues continuously without policy intervention, so the state has no mechanical need to repress gold — the FX does the adjustment.

A2.note: PASSES ALL THREE LIMBS WITH HEADROOM. Net debt ~18.8% (2025), expected to remain ~20% per the May 2026 budget; excludes Future Fund and RBA assets, so the true net position is stronger still. Commonwealth gross debt projected to peak at 35.8% of GDP in 2028-29 (PBO 2026-27 Medium-Term Budget Outlook, July 2026). Interest expense 3.5% of operating revenue in FY26 (A$27.1bn), projected 4.7% (A$42.2bn) by FY30 — the fastest-growing payment over the medium term per the PBO, and the limb to watch. CORRECTS the previous record, which carried gross_debt_gdp 0.51 against a tradingeconomics page with no stated consolidation level or vintage — neither the Commonwealth figure (~36%) nor the IMF general-government figure (~61%). That was the same defect the Canada note complained about, on the country the gate turns on.
A2.gap: The Commonwealth interest ratio is sourced to a budget commentary rather than to Budget Paper No. 1 Statement 6 directly. Upgrade the citation at the next deep rebalance. The figure is 3.5% against a 10% bar, so nothing turns on the precision.

A3.note: Gold has OVERTAKEN COAL as Australia's second-largest export by value, behind iron ore only — approximately A$68bn this financial year. The strongest single data point supporting the index thesis, and absent from v1.0.

A4.note: No gold-control regime in operation. Banking Act 1959 (Cth) Part IV — Gold ceased to be in operation on 30 January 1976 and has not been revived. Verified against primary law: the compilation endnote for every section of Part IV reads 'exp 30 Jan 1976 (s 40(3) and gaz 1976, No S17)'. Part IV has NOT been repealed and remains in the current compilation; s 40(2) permits revival. Dormant-power register below; residual risk disclosed at §11.1, not gated.
A4.compilation: C2026C00104, Compilation No. 69, compiled to 31 March 2026
A4.status: pass, with the dormant-power register disclosed at §11.1

dormant_powers.status: Not in operation since 30 Jan 1976. Not repealed, and not left to rot: ss 41, 42, 45 and 46 have been amended since suspension — penalty units and Criminal Code alignment — most recently by No 4, 2016. Parliament has kept the machinery serviceable.
dormant_powers.history: Part IV WAS in operation until 30 Jan 1976. Compulsory delivery of privately held gold to the Reserve Bank is not hypothetical in Australia; it is living memory. This is the fact the v1.0 A4 tripped on, and the reason that formulation could not be applied honestly.
dormant_powers.activation: s 40(2). Where the Governor-General is satisfied it is expedient for the protection of the currency or of the public credit of the Commonwealth, the Governor-General may by Proclamation declare that this Part — 'OR SUCH OF THE PROVISIONS OF THIS PART AS ARE SPECIFIED IN THE PROCLAMATION' — comes into operation. An executive act. Gazetted, so not silent; but no parliamentary vote, and effective on the day.

powers.power: Gold may not be taken or sent out of Australia except with the written consent of the Reserve Bank. 200 penalty units, indictable.
A holder must deliver gold to the Reserve Bank within one month. Carve-outs for small gold-coin holdings and for gold lawfully held as trade or professional working stock.
Gold delivered vests in the Reserve Bank.

THE COMPENSATION PROVISION. 'The amount to be paid for any gold delivered in pursuance of section 42 shall be an amount determined in accordance with such price as is fixed and published by the Reserve Bank or, at the option of the person delivering the gold, such amount as is determined in an action for compensation against the Reserve Bank.'

Gold may be sold only to, and bought only from, the Reserve Bank or a person it authorises in writing. This is an administered monopsony — the same instrument as the 1934 US Gold Reserve Act, held dormant.
Gold may not be worked or used in manufacture, other than gold lawfully held as trade or professional working stock.
The Reserve Bank may exempt any person from any or all of Part IV by written instrument.
powers.compensation: n/a — a discretionary relief valve, not a right

dormant_powers.two_gaps: Both were missed by the first attempt at this record and both matter. (1) s 44 reaches only gold 'delivered in pursuance of section 42'. The export ban (s 41), the monopsony (s 45) and the prohibition on working gold (s 46) carry no compensation provision anywhere in Part IV. (2) s 40(2) permits PARTIAL activation. A Proclamation naming only ss 41, 45 and 46 delivers an export ban, a Reserve Bank purchase monopsony and a manufacturing prohibition with s 44 never switched on. The compensation route is therefore not a property of Part IV; it is a property of one limb of it, and the executive chooses which limbs operate.
dormant_powers.constitutional_backstop: s 51(xxxi) requires that any Commonwealth acquisition of property be on just terms, and Part IV is Commonwealth law, so the guarantee reaches it — this is distinct from, and stronger than, the state-tenure caveat in `constitutional_note` below. Newcrest Mining v Commonwealth (1997) 190 CLR 513 is live precedent that sterilisation of mining tenements can be an acquisition attracting compensation. UNRESOLVED, and the question for counsel: Australian law distinguishes acquisition of property from mere deprivation or regulation. Compulsory delivery and vesting (ss 42-43) is plainly an acquisition. An export ban, a monopsony or a ban on working gold may be characterised as regulation, attracting no just-terms obligation at all. The compensation floor is firm for the delivery limb and genuinely contestable for the control limbs.
dormant_powers.residual_risk: Activation is a same-day executive act on a currency-protection test the executive applies to itself. If the delivery limb is activated the price is administered by the Reserve Bank, with a court action as the only route to a different number. If only the control limbs are activated there is no priced route at all. Unquantified and unpriced. §11.1.

countries.constitutional_note: s51(xxxi) requires acquisition of property on just terms, with live precedent protecting mining tenements — Newcrest Mining v Commonwealth (1997) 190 CLR 513, where sterilisation of tenements by Kakadu proclamations was held an acquisition requiring compensation. CAVEAT: s51(xxxi) binds the Commonwealth, not the States. Mining tenure is granted under the WA Mining Act 1978 and state parliaments are not subject to the guarantee. Parked as an accepted risk (§11.1); it carries most of the residual jurisdictional risk in a ~100% Australian portfolio.

countries.name: New Zealand

A2.note: Gross debt moderate, well inside the threshold on every limb. UNSOURCED to a vintage, and it stays that way deliberately: New Zealand hosts no eligible listed vehicle, so nothing turns on it. Source it before admitting any NZ-asset company, not before.
A2.gap: No figure recorded for any of the three limbs. Verdict is an assertion, not a derivation.

A3.note: Gold immaterial to NZ goods exports; dairy dominates. Low score, not a gate failure.

A4.note: No gold-control regime in operation. No dormant-power register compiled — nil exposure, so it has not been researched to the standard applied to Australia. Recorded, not verified.

countries.verdict: PASS (A1, A2, A4; low A3 score)
countries.note: No eligible listed vehicle. OceanaGold is the only material NZ gold producer and its NZ assets (Macraes, Waihi) are a minority against Haile (US, ~315 koz 2026) and Didipio (Philippines, 80%-owned). NZ remains in the eligible set should a pure-play emerge. Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 fully operational; amendments Dec 2025 and Mar 2026 expanded scope — policy direction has hardened pro-mining.

countries.name: Canada

fails_on: gross debt 105-110% of GDP against the 85% limb
federal interest 10.3% of revenue against the 10% limb
A2.note: FAILS TWO LIMBS, PASSES ONE. Gross: general government gross debt 105-110% of GDP, in the IMF's >100% cluster with Japan, Italy, Greece, France, Belgium, the UK and the US; Australia is not in that group. Interest: the federal government spent 10.3 cents of every revenue dollar on interest in 2024, and the PBO projects the federal debt-service ratio reaching 13.1% by 2030-31, its highest since 2007. Net debt PASSES and is not the basis of the exclusion: ~10% of GDP on the IMF basis, ~13% on an IMF national-accounts basis, the lowest in the G7 — but that figure is an artefact of netting CPP/QPP social-security fund assets (~29% of GDP) that are legally earmarked for pension obligations and cannot service general government debt. Excluding social-security funds, StatCan puts general government net financial liabilities at ~50% of GDP. The consolidated general government interest ratio of 8.8% also passes, and is not the test: provinces cannot impose gold controls.
A2.source_interest: Statistics Canada, Consolidated Canadian Government Finance Statistics 2024, released 21 Nov 2025 — https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/251121/dq251121b-eng.htm
A2._amendment_note: RESOLVED 19 Aug 2026, §12.2 item 4, and resolved as a RULE CHANGE rather than as a sourcing fix — read the direction carefully. A2 as written in v1.1 specified general government NET debt <= 60% and interest/revenue <= 10%. Sourced, Canada PASSES both of those: net ~10-13% (lower than Australia's ~19%) and general government interest 8.8%. Recording FAIL against a rule the evidence passes is exactly the v1.0 A4 defect — a test failing and the verdict recorded anyway. So the rule was changed instead, in the open, in the amendment record: A2 is now measured on the currency issuer and carries a gross-debt limb. Canada then fails on gross and on federal interest. Anyone reading this record is entitled to know that the exclusion survives on the amended rule and not on the original one.

A3.note: Gold a significant but not dominant export.

A4.note: No gold-control regime in operation. The Foreign Exchange Control Board regime of 1939-1951 required residents to surrender foreign exchange and gold; it ended in 1951 and no successor is in force. Historical use is disclosed, not gated (§2.1).
A4.history: Foreign Exchange Control Act 1939-1951 — the Foreign Exchange Control Board required residents to surrender foreign exchange and gold. A modern-era requisition precedent, retained as a disclosure.
A4.gap: No dormant-power register compiled. Whether Canadian current law retains latent bullion or exchange-control machinery has not been researched to the standard applied to Australia — the Currency Act, the Bank of Canada Act and the Emergencies Act 1988 would be the places to look, the last of which was invoked in February 2022 to direct financial institutions to freeze accounts without a court order and is therefore a recently-exercised financial-control power rather than a dormant one. Item 4 is now worked and A2 still excludes Canada, so this register stays uncompiled by decision, not by oversight. It becomes required work the moment Canada's A2 verdict is revisited.

countries.verdict: FAIL — A2 (gross debt limb and currency-issuer interest limb)
countries.note: Consequence: Red Lake (Evolution) and Sugar Zone (Vault) are ineligible ounces. Agnico Eagle excluded at entity level.

countries.name: Finland

A1.note: Euro member. No monetary sovereignty, no independent devaluation channel, and no exit. In an EU-level debt event Finland receives whatever the ECB and Council decide — Cyprus 2013 and Greece 2015 are the proof of concept for capital controls imposed on a member state.

A2.note: UNTESTED, changed from a v1.1 FAIL. Gross debt approximately 80% of GDP and rising sits INSIDE the 85% limb, so the only sourced limb does not fail Finland, and the net-debt and interest limbs are unsourced. A2 no longer carries this exclusion and it would be dishonest to keep recording one. Finland fails A1 outright on euro membership — not a test a member state can pass — so the country verdict is unchanged and the basis is A1 alone. Source the remaining limbs only if a Finland-exposed candidate ever appears; none does today.
A2.gap: Net debt/GDP and interest/revenue unsourced. Immaterial while A1 excludes Finland.

A4.note: No gold-control regime in operation. No dormant-power register compiled — nil exposure since the Rupert delisting. Recorded, not verified.

countries.note: v1.0 treated Finland as eligible. Moot in practice — Rupert Resources, the only Finland-exposed constituent, delisted 16 Jun 2026 into Agnico Eagle. Separately, the Mined Minerals Tax (Act 1361/2025, effective 1 Jan 2026) raised the ad valorem rate on metallic ores 4.2x from 0.6% to 2.5% — not a Tier A failure but a 4.2x repricing of the state's claim, and exactly the fiscal-variance behaviour Tier B B2 exists to capture.

countries.name: United States

A1.note: Global reserve currency issuer. Unique motive — managing devaluation while defending reserve status — and unique tools.

A2.note: Net debt ~100% of GDP rising to just under 120% by 2029. Gross 126% in 2026 rising to 142% by 2031 — the largest absolute deterioration among advanced economies. Primary deficits averaging 6.7% of GDP for 2027-2031, against the ~3.5% associated with debt stabilisation.

A3.note: US gold output ~155-170 t/yr is immaterial to exports and the sector is politically small. No constituency defends it.

A4.note: No gold-control regime in operation. EO 6102 and the Gold Reserve Act monopsony are spent; private gold ownership has been lawful since 31 December 1974 (Pub. L. 93-373), and WPB Order L-208 was rescinded in 1945. The United States therefore PASSES the present-tense A4. That is the uncomfortable and correct result — see `why_this_passes_and_it_does_not_matter`.
A4.history: EO 6102 (Apr 1933) confiscated privately held gold. Gold Reserve Act (Jan 1934) revalued $20.67 to $35 AFTER the state took possession, and required newly mined domestic gold be sold to the Treasury at the official price — monopsony, not seizure. WPB Order L-208 (Oct 1942) ordered non-essential gold mines shut outright to redirect labour and equipment, without compensation. The heaviest historical disclosure in this file, and it is a disclosure, not a gate.
A4.why_this_passes_and_it_does_not_matter: A4 tests machinery in operation, and none is operating. Note what this means for the gate's strength: a DORMANT EO 6102 would also pass, because it was a public executive instrument and surrender was paid at a published statutory price. That weakness is accepted deliberately (§2.1). Any A4 strong enough to catch a dormant EO 6102 also catches Banking Act Part IV — which is to say it catches Australia and leaves the index holding nothing. The United States is excluded by A1 and A2: reserve issuance and insolvency are where the motive the index actually fears is measured. A4 was never what kept the US out; it only looked that way.
A4.gap: No dormant-power register compiled for current US law — TWEA s 5(b), IEEPA and 31 U.S.C. ch. 51 have not been read to the standard applied to Australian Part IV. Immaterial while A1 and A2 exclude the US, and it would take an A1 and A2 reversal to make it matter.

countries.thesis_note: The realistic mechanism is not nationalisation of producers — US mine output at ~$20bn/yr against a $37tn debt stock is fiscally irrelevant. The prize is the stock: 8,133 t in the Treasury's gold certificate account still carried at $42.22/oz. Revaluing that requires touching no mining company. The risk to producers is monopsony purchase at an administered price, plus capital and export controls. Consequence for the index: Pogo (Northern Star) is ineligible ounces, and every US-domiciled producer is out.
